blocks.text: A moving object possesses a quality by virtue of which it exerts a force on anything that tries to stop it: the faster the object travels, the harder it is to stop, and of two objects moving with the same velocity the more massive is more difficult to stop. Newton called this quality the quantity of motion of the body; it is now called the linear momentum p of the body.

blocks.title: Linear momentum
blocks.text: p = m v ... (2.25), where v is the velocity of the mass m. Linear momentum is a vector quantity with the direction of the velocity. Its SI unit is kilogram metre per second (kg m s^-1), which can also be expressed as newton second (N s).
Momentum and Newton's second law of motion

Consider a body of mass m moving with initial velocity vi; an external force F acts on it for time t, after which its velocity becomes vf. The acceleration produced is a = (vf - vi)/t, and by Newton's second law a = F/m. Equating the two expressions, F/m = (vf - vi)/t, or F x t = m vf - m vi ... (2.26), where m vi is the initial momentum and m vf the final momentum. Equation (2.26) shows that the change in momentum equals the product of the force and the time for which it is applied. This form of the second law is more general than F = ma, because it can be extended to cases where the mass also changes as the body accelerates: as a rocket accelerates it loses mass, because its fuel is burnt and ejected to provide greater thrust. From (2.26), F = (m vf - m vi)/t, so the second law can also be stated in terms of momentum: the time rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the applied force.

Sometimes the applied force is not constant and acts for a very short time, as when a bat hits a cricket ball and the force varies from instant to instant during the collision. It is then more convenient to deal with the product of force and time (F x t) instead of either quantity alone. The product of the average force F that acts during time t is called the impulse: impulse = F x t = m vf - m vi ... (2.27).

blocks.title: Example 2.6
blocks.text: A 1500 kg car has its velocity reduced from 20 m s^-1 to 15 m s^-1 in 3.0 s. How large was the average retarding force? Solution: using Eq. (2.27), F x t = m vf - m vi, F x 3.0 s = 1500 kg x 15 m s^-1 - 1500 kg x 20 m s^-1, so F = -2500 kg m s^-2 = -2500 N = -2.5 kN. The negative sign indicates that the force is a retarding one.

An isolated system is one on which no external agency exerts any force; for example, the molecules of a gas enclosed in a glass vessel at constant temperature form an isolated system: they collide with one another because of their random motion, but being enclosed by the vessel no external agency can exert a force on them. Consider an isolated system of two smooth hard interacting balls of masses m1 and m2 moving along the same straight line in the same direction with velocities v1 and v2. They collide, and after the collision m1 moves with velocity v1' and m2 with v2' in the same direction (Fig. 2.9). To find the change in momentum of m1, from Eq. (2.27), F x t = m1 v1' - m1 v1; similarly for m2, F' x t = m2 v2' - m2 v2. Adding, (F + F') t = (m1 v1' - m1 v1) + (m2 v2' - m2 v2). Since the action force F is equal and opposite to the reaction force F', F' = -F, or F + F' = 0, so the left-hand side is zero: 0 = (m1 v1' - m1 v1) + (m2 v2' - m2 v2). In other words, the change in momentum of the first ball plus the change in momentum of the second ball is zero, or m1 v1 + m2 v2 = m1 v1' + m2 v2' ... (2.28): the total initial momentum of the system before the collision equals the total final momentum after it, so the total change in momentum of the isolated two-ball system is zero.

For such a group of objects, if one object within the group experiences a force there must exist an equal but opposite reaction force on another object in the same group; as a result, the change in momentum of the group as a whole is always zero. This is the law of conservation of momentum: the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant. In applying the law we must remember that the momentum of a body is a vector quantity.

blocks.title: Example 2.7
blocks.text: Two spherical balls of 2.0 kg and 3.0 kg are moving towards each other with velocities 6.0 m s^-1 and 4 m s^-1. What must be the velocity of the smaller ball after the collision if the velocity of the bigger ball is 3.0 m s^-1? Solution: as the balls move towards one another their velocities have opposite signs; take the direction of the 2 kg ball as positive and that of the 3 kg ball as negative. Momentum before the collision: m1 v1 + m2 v2 = 2 kg x 6 m s^-1 + 3 kg x (-4 m s^-1) = 12 kg m s^-1 - 12 kg m s^-1 = 0. Momentum after: m1 v1' + m2 v2' = 2 kg x v1' + 3 kg x (-3) m s^-1. From conservation, 0 = 2 kg x v1' - 9 kg m s^-1, so v1' = 4.5 m s^-1.

blocks.prompt: A 20 g ball hits the wall of a squash court with a constant force of 50 N for 0.50 s; find the impulse. A footballer applies an average force of 240 N for 0.25 s; find the change in momentum and its direction (numerical problems 2.7, 2.8). Why do seatbelts and helmets reduce injury?
blocks.explanation: Impulse = F x t = 50 N x 0.50 s = 25 N s (the mass is not needed). Change in momentum = 240 N x 0.25 s = 60 N s = 60 kg m s^-1, in the direction of the applied force, the direction the ball was kicked. A helmet's padding and a seatbelt lengthen the time over which the momentum change happens, so for the same change in momentum the average force F = (m vf - m vi)/t is smaller.

items: p = mv (kg m s^-1 = N s), a vector. F t = m vf - m vi: force = rate of change of momentum (more general than F = ma, allows changing mass). Impulse = F t = change in momentum (Example 2.6: -2.5 kN).
Conservation: in an isolated system F' = -F, so m1 v1 + m2 v2 = m1 v1' + m2 v2'; the total linear momentum of an isolated system stays constant (vector sum). Example 2.7: v1' = 4.5 m s^-1.
